fields.h1: Charles Spurgeon: The Prince of Preachers
fields.meta_title: Charles Spurgeon: The Prince of Preachers
fields.description: Charles Spurgeon preached the gospel to millions, cared for the poor, and suffered deeply — all to lift up Jesus Christ. The life and legacy of the Prince of Preachers.
fields.body_html:
Charles Haddon Spurgeon has been called the “Prince of Preachers,” and few titles have been better earned. For nearly four decades in Victorian London he preached the gospel to thousands every week, filling the largest auditorium of his day, and his printed sermons went out by the million to every corner of the earth. Yet Spurgeon was no distant celebrity; he was a warm-hearted pastor, a tireless worker for the poor, a sufferer who knew deep pain, and above all a man in love with Jesus Christ. His one aim, from first to last, was the aim Paul named: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2). His life and legacy still stir Christians to love the Saviour and proclaim him boldly.

A remarkable conversion

Spurgeon was born in 1834 into a family of Congregational ministers, but for all his religious upbringing he remained, by his own account, under deep conviction of sin and without peace. Then, on a snowy Sunday in January 1850, unable to reach his usual church, the teenaged Spurgeon turned into a tiny Primitive Methodist chapel. The regular preacher was absent, and a humble, unpolished layman stood up to preach on the text, “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22).

The simple man had little to say and soon ran short, but he fixed his eyes on the young stranger and urged him to look to Christ. In that moment Spurgeon looked, and was saved. He never forgot it, and it shaped his whole ministry: salvation is by simply looking to Jesus, and the plainest preaching of Christ can save a soul. From that unlikely beginning came one of the greatest preaching ministries in the history of the church.

The Prince of Preachers

Spurgeon’s gifts were extraordinary. Called to pastor a London congregation while barely nineteen, he saw it grow so rapidly that ever-larger buildings had to be found, until the Metropolitan Tabernacle was built to seat around five thousand — and it was filled twice every Sunday for decades. He preached without gimmicks, in plain and vivid English, with a voice that could reach vast crowds and a wit and warmth that held them. But the secret of his power was not his eloquence; it was his message. He preached Christ crucified, unashamed of the gospel, “for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Romans 1:16).

His sermons were taken down and printed each week, and they sold in the millions across the world and in many languages — the most widely read sermons in history. Through the printed page his ministry reached places his voice never could, and it reaches still. He fulfilled the charge to “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2), pouring out the gospel with a passion that never cooled.

More than a preacher

Spurgeon was far more than a Sunday orator. He founded a college to train preachers, an orphanage to care for fatherless children, and colportage work to spread Christian books; he wrote commentaries, edited a magazine, and produced devotional works still treasured today. He carried the weight of a huge congregation and countless ministries, laboring as one who could say with Paul, “I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God” (Acts 20:24).

His compassion for the poor was practical and tireless. In an age of great poverty he used his fame and his resources to feed, house, educate, and lift the needy, believing that a gospel that saved souls must also serve bodies. The breadth of his labours astonishes even now, and all of it flowed from a heart captured by the love of Christ.

A man acquainted with suffering

For all his success, Spurgeon’s life was marked by deep suffering, and this is part of what makes him so helpful a companion. He endured painful physical illness for many years — gout and other ailments that often laid him low — and he battled seasons of profound depression. He was also fiercely attacked: slandered in the press, and later embroiled in bitter controversy when he stood, at great personal cost, for the truth of the gospel against those who would water it down.

Yet in his suffering Spurgeon learned to trust the goodness of God, and he ministered out of his wounds to a hurting world. He spoke often of learning to submit to God’s providence even when it was painful, trusting the wisdom and love behind every trial. His frank honesty about depression has been a lifeline to countless believers who suffer as he did, showing that a mighty servant of God can walk through deep darkness and still hold fast. He knew from experience the promise that “those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:5).

The heart of his message

Whatever his subject, Spurgeon always came round to the cross. He preached the free grace of God to sinners with such warmth and clarity that hardened hearts melted. He would plead with his hearers to trust Christ, holding out the gospel not as a demand but as a gift, and refusing to let any sinner think themselves beyond mercy. His little book on salvation, written for the anxious and the seeking, has led many thousands to faith, and it breathes his lifelong conviction that the way to God is open to all who will simply believe.

He never tired of the message that “God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). Though he preached, like Paul, “Christ crucified” — “a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” but “the power of God” to those being saved (1 Corinthians 1:23–24) — he preached it with such joy and tenderness that it drew multitudes to the Saviour.

A wealth of written treasure

Spurgeon’s pen was as busy as his pulpit. Beyond his weekly sermons, he produced a vast body of writing that continues to nourish believers today. He laboured for some twenty years over a monumental commentary on the Psalms, gathering not only his own reflections but the choicest comments of centuries of Christian writers. He wrote homely, practical wisdom for ordinary working people, gathering the plain sayings of country folk and turning them to spiritual profit. And he produced devotional readings that have accompanied countless believers through their mornings and evenings ever since.

What unites all these works is the same warm, vivid, Christ-exalting spirit that filled his preaching. Spurgeon never wrote to display his learning but to feed his readers, and his writing has the same directness and tenderness as his spoken word. To read him is to sit under a pastor who loved his people and loved his Lord, and who wanted nothing more than to bring the two together. It is little wonder that, more than a century on, his books remain among the most widely read of any preacher who ever lived.

His enduring legacy

Spurgeon died in 1892, worn out in his fifties by a lifetime of labour, but his ministry did not end. His sermons and books continue to be read, preached, and translated across the world, still leading people to Christ more than a century after his death. He remains a model of Christ-centred preaching, pastoral compassion, and faithful endurance through suffering.

It is worth remembering, too, that Spurgeon accomplished all of this in a comparatively short life, worn out by his fifties. He crammed into those years the labour of several ordinary lifetimes, and he did it while carrying chronic pain and recurring depression. That such fruitfulness could flow from such a suffering vessel is itself a testimony to the grace that sustained him — the treasure of the gospel carried, as always, in a fragile jar of clay so that the power might be seen to be God’s.

What makes Spurgeon endure is not his fame but his faithfulness — his single-minded devotion to lifting up Jesus Christ. He would have been the first to deflect all praise from himself to his Master. His life urges every believer, whether preacher or not, to be unashamed of the gospel, to spend themselves for others, to trust God in suffering, and above all to look, and to point others to look, to the crucified and risen Christ who saved a doubting boy in a snowbound chapel and made him a blessing to the world. If God could take a boy converted in a snowbound backstreet chapel and make him the most fruitful preacher of his age, he can take any ordinary life surrendered to him and use it beyond all imagining — for the power was never in the preacher, but in the gospel he preached.
